cases.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: arctangent of the point (1,1), which is pi/4
cases.expected_note: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 0.785398163. Independently verified in Python: Excel's argument order is ATAN2(x_num, y_num), so this is math.atan2(1, 1) = 0.7853981633974483 = pi/4 -> 0.785398163 at 9 dp

cases.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: arctangent of the point (-1,-1), which is -3*pi/4
cases.expected_note: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as -2.35619449. Independently verified: math.atan2(-1, -1) = -2.356194490192345 = -3*pi/4 -> -2.35619449 at 8 dp. This case also pins the documented argument ORDER: a function taking (y, x) instead would still return -3*pi/4 here, but the first-quadrant and x=0 cases below separate the two conventions

cases.description: The same example converted to degrees with the DEGREES function, as the page's fourth example does
cases.expected_note: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as -135. Independently verified: -3*pi/4 radians = -135 degrees exactly

cases.description: An x-coordinate of zero, which the documentation explicitly allows
cases.expected_note: Excel documents "ATAN2(a,b) equals ATAN(b/a), except that a can equal 0 in ATAN2". With x_num = 0 and y_num = 1 the point is straight up the y-axis, so the angle from the x-axis is pi/2. Independently verified: math.atan2(1, 0) = 1.5707963267948966 -> 1.570796327 at 9 dp

cases.description: Both coordinates zero, which has no defined angle
cases.expected_note: Excel documents: "If both x_num and y_num are 0, ATAN2 returns the #DIV/0! error value." Note this is #DIV/0!, not the #NUM! that most out-of-domain math arguments produce
